nodes.name: Curious reader
nodes.text: Saw the headlines (websites offline, governments warning) and wants to know what happened and whether to worry.

nodes.name: Website owner
nodes.text: Runs a small business, charity or club website (often WordPress) on a hosting plan, and is not a developer.

nodes.name: Board member or executive
nodes.text: Sits on a board or leadership team; will be asked whether the organisation is exposed and must not repeat a wrong number.

nodes.name: Project or programme manager
nodes.text: Runs a delivery plan that depends on websites or web apps, and needs to know what this does to the schedule.

nodes.name: CFO
nodes.text: Owns the money: the cost of downtime, the cost of a breach, and whether insurance responds.

nodes.name: Data protection officer
nodes.text: Advises the controller on GDPR; decides with it whether an incident is a personal data breach, whether the 72-hour clock has started, and what goes on the record.

nodes.name: CISO
nodes.text: Accountable for security risk; must report exposure and evidence of non-compromise to the board.

nodes.name: CTO
nodes.text: Owns the platform and the engineering time; needs the patch order, what breaks, and what to change next.

nodes.name: Journalist
nodes.text: Reporting the story; needs numbers that hold up, quotes that are on the page they are attributed to, and the order of events.

nodes.name: Communications team
nodes.text: Writes the organisation's statement and answers the press; needs what is safe to say and what will be asked.

nodes.name: Security lead
nodes.text: Runs the response: patch order, mitigations, monitoring and the offline call.

nodes.name: Head of AppSec
nodes.text: Owns application security across many teams; needs scope, settings and the pipeline change.

nodes.name: PHP or platform engineer
nodes.text: Runs the servers and containers; needs versions, SAPIs, ini settings and commands.

nodes.name: Developer
nodes.text: Writes PHP applications; wants to know whether their code is the problem and what they can do.

nodes.name: Security researcher
nodes.text: Studies vulnerabilities; wants the bug classes, what was demonstrated against what, and the open technical questions.

nodes.name: Analyst or policy advisor
nodes.text: Advises on policy or markets; wants what this says about disclosure, AI-assisted discovery and how agencies responded.

nodes.name: Someone else runs code on your web server
nodes.text: An unauthenticated request can turn into code running as the web worker, before any application code runs. Demonstrated against mod_php; FPM susceptible, the two primary accounts differ on a complete exploit.

nodes.name: What the server holds is taken
nodes.text: Code running as the worker reaches whatever the worker can: configuration, database credentials, sessions, user records. No named organisation has confirmed this happening through php2shell.

nodes.name: Pulling the plug costs you
nodes.text: The advice to take systems offline when patching is not possible turned into councils, police, government portals and wikis going dark, as a precaution.

nodes.name: Your version gets no fix
nodes.text: PHP 8.1 and older are out of support: source backports, no release, and the CVE records do not list them.

nodes.name: The fix is not the end
nodes.text: A report that the 8.5.12 fix may be incomplete, and a vendor's view that patching the demonstrated paths does not make the bailout mechanism safe.

nodes.name: The firewall in front is not enough
nodes.text: Edge rules shipped before disclosure and every vendor calls them a stopgap; attackers mutated payloads, and a rule sees only traffic routed through it.

nodes.name: You cannot tell whether you were hit
nodes.text: The default web log records neither the content type nor the body, and a clean log proves little. The absence of a confirmed victim is a fact about the evidence so far.

nodes.name: Attackers had it before the patch
nodes.text: The CVE IDs leaked a day early, a demonstration video circulated, patched images shipped before the embargo, and attempts reached honeypots days before disclosure.

nodes.name: Deciding on the wrong numbers
nodes.text: 70% of the Internet, CVSS 10.0, disclosed on 22 October: figures in circulation that the primary sources do not carry.

nodes.name: The bug is in the engine, not in your code
nodes.text: Two memory-safety failures in how PHP recovers from an error, reachable by any request.

nodes.name: The fix is a redesign
nodes.text: Out-of-memory handling rebuilt: 389 files, a soft and a hard limit, globals reset, parsing bounded.

nodes.name: Found with AI, three times over
nodes.text: Calif, OpenAI and Wiz found it in August; a 2024 audit had seen it and left it.

nodes.name: Coordinated disclosure broke
nodes.text: The IDs leaked with a wrong score, a video went out, the release moved forward a day.

nodes.name: The numbers do not measure the same thing
nodes.text: Websites, hosts, the Internet: each figure counts something different.

nodes.name: Millions of attempts, no confirmed breach
nodes.text: Probing at scale, honeypot hits before disclosure, and no named victim.

nodes.name: Pulling the plug
nodes.text: Agencies said offline as the last step; governments, councils and wikis did it.

nodes.name: CVE-2026-109618: RCE via OOM corruption
nodes.text: An out-of-memory condition during request handling could leave request memory in an uninitialised state that later cleanup reads. CVSS v4.0 9.2. GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w.

nodes.name: CVE-2026-109619: RCE via stale global state
nodes.text: Global state that referenced request memory was not always reset, so a later request on the same worker could read freed memory. CVSS v4.0 9.2. GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp.

nodes.name: The fix commit 3584a98bd
nodes.text: "Avoid state corruption via bailout", by Arnaud Le Blanc with Ilija Tovilo, Jakub Zelenka, Nora Dossche and Nicolas Grekas. Authored 2026-10-18 15:26 UTC; public on the branches 2026-10-21 14:06 UTC. 389 files, +10,689 / -976.

nodes.name: A soft memory limit that no longer jumps
nodes.text: At the memory limit the allocator stops using the longjmp bailout; it queues a delayed error and lets the allocation proceed, so the fatal is raised later with request state intact.

nodes.name: A hard limit that ends the process cleanly
nodes.text: A new memory_hard_limit_percent sets a ceiling above memory_limit; reaching it ends the worker with _exit(), leaving no cleanup to corrupt. zend_mm_panic also uses _exit now.

nodes.name: An orderly unwind at the next safe point
nodes.text: The queued error is handled at a VM safe point: it throws an UnwindExit that unwinds the PHP frames in order before the fatal, rather than a C longjmp across half-built state.

nodes.name: Request globals reset so nothing survives a failure
nodes.text: Shutdown and deactivate paths set freed pointers to NULL or UNDEF, 'may be accessed before php_request_startup()', so a later request cannot find stale state.

nodes.name: Bounded, deduplicated request parsing
nodes.text: A new max_multipart_body_parts caps the number of parts the body parser accepts; the multipart header parser keeps only the two headers it uses and ignores duplicates; the session upload-progress callback is changed.

nodes.name: Allocations that may fail instead of abort
nodes.text: Allocation paths a caller can tolerate failing become 'fallible' and return NULL rather than jumping, which is what lets the new tests exercise the OOM handling at any allocation.
